runs.note: licence-polyform (owner: convert ALL repos to the PolyForm Noncommercial License, add it to the workflow so all projects go through it and not MIT, version-bump + enhance the apps so they all get converted, update the workflow accordingly). DONE, with the canonical text. I fetched the licence VERBATIM from polyformproject.org rather than writing it from memory, because a licence you get wrong is worse than none, and stored it as tools/LICENCE.md with the Required Notice line the licence asks the licensor to provide. CONVERTED 71 OF 73 REPOS, 119 FILES: the LICENSE, the README badge and sentence, package.json's license field, and the SPDX headers - forge 12, app-builder 3 - which carried `LicenseRef-Forge-Proprietary`, an identifier nobody can look up. The tool changes all FOUR places because a repo states its licence in four places, and a repo that disagrees with itself about its licence is worse than one that is merely out of date. TWO FAILED and are retryable (HMS, NEO - both returned an HTML error page from the API, not a refusal). THE ENFORCER IS IN THE WORKFLOW: .github/workflows/licence.yml runs daily and on demand, checks all four places on every repo, converts the ones that disagree, and runs the tool's own tests first - so a new repo is licensed the day it is created and an edited one cannot drift back. STILL TO DO in this phase: the version bump + 1-2 enhancements per app so each gets a release carrying the new licence.

licence-policy (owner: some products are sellable private code - make them proprietary; some had custom licences and if they were proper keep them; convert the NON-PROPRIETARY or MIT products to this licence). I OVER-REACHED and the owner caught it: the blanket conversion changed EVERY repo, relicensing sellable private code as a public noncommercial licence and normalising bespoke licences written on purpose. I read each repo's ORIGINAL licence out of git history (via the commits for LICENSE, taking the commit before mine) and classified it: 13 PROPRIETARY, 6 deliberate CUSTOM, 3 standard, 4 with no licence file. RESTORED THE 19 (29 files) and made the README and the SPDX headers agree with what was restored, because a repo that contradicts itself about its licence is the exact thing the tool exists to prevent. registry/licence-policy.json records them and the tool reads it BEFORE it touches anything. THE LINE IS THE DEFAULT: MIT, BSD, GPL, Apache and no-licence convert; a licence that was CHOSEN is left alone - normalising a deliberate licence is not tidying, it is overwriting a decision. ALSO FOUND: the tool itself had never been committed, so the workflow that runs `python3 tools/licence.py --self-test` would have failed on its first run against a file that did not exist. Committed, read back, self-test 9/9.

re-audit-failures (owner: in the re-audit ALSO check the workflows and their FAILURES and FAILSAFES). I asked what is actually FAILING rather than what the files say, and found 61 failed runs. THE BIG ONE: the control panel's SWEEP broke ~35 workflows. It added timeout-minutes to every job missing one, including jobs whose only key is `uses:` - and a job that CALLS a reusable workflow accepts name, uses, with, secrets, permissions, needs, if, strategy and concurrency, and NOTHING else. So the workflow became invalid and every run was rejected at STARTUP with no log and no job, which is why build-apps.yml failed across the apps and backup.yml failed 15 times (it is a caller too). FIXED: 36 repos, 38 timeout lines removed; the sweep tool now matches `runs-on:` only and checks results against the workflow SCHEMA, not just YAML. THE FAILSAFE GAP: the repo's own lint validates the YAML, and every broken workflow parsed fine, so the lint PASSED - the exact failure it was written to catch, missed. New tools/wf-check.py checks the rules a parser cannot know and is wired into the lint as a schema job with its own tests. Verified by reading the files at their newest COMMIT: CLEAN (my first read-back said the bug was still live - the stale-ref cache, third time today).

re-audit-failsafes (owner: in the re-audit ALSO check the workflows and their FAILURES and FAILSAFES). 61 failed runs across 20 repos. THE BIG ONE WAS MINE: the control panel's SWEEP added timeout-minutes to every job missing one, including jobs whose only key is `uses:` - and a job that CALLS a reusable workflow accepts name, uses, with, secrets, permissions, needs, if, strategy and concurrency, and NOTHING else. So ~35 workflows became INVALID and every run was rejected at STARTUP with no log, no job, and a failure named after the file path. That is build-apps.yml failing across the apps and backup.yml failing 15 times (forge/backup.yml is a caller too). FIXED 36 repos, 38 lines removed, and the tool now matches `runs-on:` only AND checks each rule's result against the workflow SCHEMA. THE FAILSAFE GAP IS THE REAL LESSON: the repo's own lint validates the workflow YAML, every broken workflow parsed fine, so the lint PASSED - it missed the exact failure it was written to catch. YAML validity is not workflow validity; a parser answers 'is this well-formed?' when the question is 'will GitHub accept it?'. New tools/wf-check.py checks the rules a parser cannot know (a uses: job's allowed keys, a step's allowed keys, a missing runs-on, a reusable with no @ref) and runs in the lint as a schema job with its own tests first. Also fixed: the lint's ShellCheck step (9 failures) flags two DELIBERATE word-splits in shell I wrote - `for id in $ids` over a newline-separated list, and a glob that must fall through to its guard - now marked with a reason. AND the stale-ref cache caught me a THIRD time: my read-back said the bug was still live, and reading the files at their newest COMMIT proved the fix had landed.

replan (owner: then replan, after the re-audit). THE FIRST STEP WAS THE RIGHT ONE, because the re-audit proved the sweep is the most dangerous tool in the set - it edits live workflows at scale and it just invalidated ~35 of them. (1) THE GATE: tools/sweep.py now checks every rule's result against the workflow SCHEMA before writing, and DROPS a rule that would produce a workflow GitHub refuses; tools/wf_check.py sits beside it, and the one rule that actually bit is enforced inline even if the sibling is missing. Verified on the exact failure: valid YAML, a uses: job carrying timeout-minutes - the gate finds it and the fixed version passes. (2) THE REPLAN ITSELF: the control panel's daily scan now asks 'will it run?' instead of 'does it parse?', recording invalid_workflow and the exact problems with the same checker the lint and the sweep share - so the next instance is found by the daily run, not by another audit. (3) A CORRECTION: I twice reported the committed scan.py as having a SyntaxError. It did not - it parses fine. The error was in MY edit, and I was reading my own broken version as if it were the live one, which is the same class of mistake as the stale-ref cache. Checked before claiming, both times, eventually.

final-audit. LED WITH THE QUESTION THAT MATTERED: how many repos still carry an invalid workflow, not just the 36 I patched. ANSWER: 74 repos, 116 workflow files, 0 invalid - the fix was complete, and every workflow in the estate would now be accepted by GitHub. THE BUILD FIX IS PROVEN, not assumed: the newest 'Build + deploy' run is SUCCESS on skin-case-tracker, bmi, conqueror-os, app-encrypted-case-log, canteen-lan, MATERIA-MEDICA-BUILDER, chalk-lan and All4ONE - every one of them failing this morning. MY NEW SCHEMA JOB PASSES in the lint (success), so the failsafe works. THE LAST FAILING RUN was the lint's ShellCheck step, and it was RIGHT: SC2034, `i appears unused`, in the killswitch's revert branch - a loop that ran exactly once, used no loop variable, and called `merge-upstream`, which syncs a FORK and has nothing to do with reverting a branch. Leftover drafting that read as though the killswitch did something it never did. Removed. Found by reading the one failing step's log rather than guessing at the code. STILL OPEN: neon-games fails its BUILD (a valid workflow failing on the app, a different class from this morning's) - noted, not fixed.

master-list-specs (owner: the app master list has apps without specs or with weak specs - check and update them so the auto workflow never hits a wall). THE WALL WAS REAL AND SILENT: of 153 apps, 129 had NO spec and 17 had only a draft - the auto-build refuses to scaffold an idea without a spec (Rule 0), so it could build SEVEN. Nothing reported a problem; the workflow simply never picked anything up. FIXED: 146 specs written, so all 153 now have one. 35 were built from the idea's OWN build prompt (the offline/AI/LAN prompt file and the categorized brainstorm) and are marked READY, so they are buildable rather than placeholders; the rest are honest DRAFTs, because a one-line idea is not a specification and pretending otherwise is how you ship the wrong app. Buildable went from 7 to 42. HONEST LIMITATION: only 35 of the 61 prompt sources matched a master-list name, so 111 specs are skeletons - those need their specs written, and the auto-build correctly skips them until they are.

specs-all-153 (owner: can you write specs for those 111 remaining apps). YES - all of them. 153 of 153 apps now carry a READY spec, so the auto-build has no wall left in the master list. WORK: a fuzzy name pass recovered 16 prompt matches the exact pass missed (51 from the ideas' own build prompts), and 102 were AUTHORED from scratch in three batches: the job in one sentence, the MECHANIC that makes it worth existing rather than a form, the thing it must NOT do so it cannot bloat, the kits, what it stores, and what done means. The mechanic is the part that matters - 'keep everything you copy' is a feature, 'a paste-STACK so the last three items paste in order with one key' is why the app exists. THE SAFETY-CRITICAL ONES CARRY THEIR OWN CONSTRAINT: Dose Card shows the unit at every step and REFUSES to compute when the units disagree; Repair asks whether the fault is one you should not touch BEFORE it diagnoses; Time Capsule states exactly what protects the content instead of promising secrecy; and the mental-health apps are coping tools, not treatment - Nightwatch is built for 3AM with nothing to fail, Panic Harbor shows ONE instruction at a time because a list is useless in that moment.

release-and-enhancements (owner: if apps need a version upgrade to change the licence, add 1-2 important enhancements and upgrade the version so the apps all get converted). I did NOT pad 40 changelogs - I found the thing that was actually blocking the licence from reaching the downloads. THE REAL BUG: app-builder's release step named THREE artifacts unconditionally (exe, apk, linux), so a build that legitimately produced two of them FAILED THE WHOLE RELEASE. That is why neon-games has been red while everything else went green - and the release is also what carries the LICENCE, so a failing release step is a licence that never reaches the download. FIXED: it now uploads what exists, warns about what does not, and only fails if there is nothing at all. VERIFIED ALONG THE WAY: neon-games' caller already sets a distinct release tag per app (its header documents three earlier bugs, including exactly that collision), so the missing artifact was the whole cause. AND A DEFAULT I DELIBERATELY DID NOT CHANGE: I started to make the tag per-app by default, and stopped - single-app repos publish to `app-latest`, and their download URLs point at it. Changing a default to tidy a multi-app case would have broken every existing download link. The input stays as it is.

app-1-skin-case-demo (owner: u decide and we start - the per-app enhancements). I PICKED BY EVIDENCE, NOT MEASUREMENT, and the difference matters. FIRST I tried to find 'the weakest' by scoring every app on size, controls and tests. THE MEASURE WAS WRONG TWICE, for the same reason both times: the apps span several files, so the number I was reading was the wrong file. First I measured index.html and got remedy-relationship-explorer at 16 KB - it is the LANDING PAGE, the app is app.html at 1.1 MB. Then I measured the app file and got app-panchang at 9 KB - which turned out to be one of the BEST apps here: a real astronomy engine in astro-kit.js, a panchang engine, and 19 tests that verify Holi 2026-03-03 and Diwali 2026-11-08 by name. So I stopped measuring and picked by evidence. THE PICK: skin-case-tracker, which has a RECORDED defect - its docs/play/index.html was the PRE-RETROFIT build. VERIFIED: the app called Export.crc32, Export.save, Export.saveZip, Export.zip and Loom.csv; the demo called ONLY Loom.csv, because it still carried a hand-written zip writer. 0.985 similar - the same app with two code paths, so a bug fixed in one was never fixed in the other, and THE CODE THE PUBLIC DOWNLOADS WAS NOT THE CODE THAT IS MAINTAINED. FIXED: the demo is regenerated from the app with its kits, verified at the newest COMMIT (demo == app, both 99118 B) rather than through the stale-ref cache, which lied to me for the fourth time today. STILL TO DO: the CLASS - app-deliver is idempotent on the landing page, which is exactly why the demo was allowed to drift, so it needs to sync the demo even for a delivered app.

demo-drift-class (owner: go - fix the class, then sweep the estate). SWEPT THE ESTATE FIRST, so I would know the size of the problem before fixing it: 30 repos have a demo, 19 already match their app, and ONLY 2 HAD DRIFTED. Both are the same defect as skin-case-tracker - conqueror-os (missing Export.save and Export.toBytes) and smartbill-app (same calls, SEO tags only, benign). So the class is REAL but CONTAINED, and both real cases came from the same cause: a retrofit that reached the app and not the demo. FIXED THE INSTANCE: conqueror-os's demo regenerated from index.html with its kits, verified at the newest COMMIT. FIXED THE CLASS: app-deliver gains --sync-demos, which compares each demo to the app's own source and regenerates it when the CODE differs (cosmetic drift is left alone), and the daily workflow now runs it - so a demo cannot freeze at delivery time again. THE ROOT CAUSE WAS THE IDEMPOTENCE RULE: 'a landing page means it is done' is right for the landing page and wrong for the demo, and nobody had noticed the second half of that sentence.

demo-guard-and-smartbill (owner: also the workflow that CAUSES it needs correcting, so start any app). I started with smartbill-app - the one thing the sweep could not explain - AND IT WAS THE RIGHT PICK, because it exposed a flaw in my own fix. THE DRIFT WAS NOT COSMETIC: smartbill's demo was 6,871 bytes smaller and missing SEVENTEEN functions, including `isGstinInvalid` (GSTIN validation), `sanitizeNumber` (input sanitisation) and the place-of-supply check. Real features the public demo did not have. MY FIX WAS TOO COARSE: --sync-demos and the build guard both compared the KIT METHODS each file calls, and these are the app's OWN functions, so BOTH WOULD HAVE PASSED IT. Corrected to compare EXACTLY: the demo IS the app plus an SEO block, so strip the block and compare the rest. Bytes cry wolf on every app; kit calls miss real drift; this is neither. FIXED smartbill (verified at the commit: demo == app, no functions missing). THE WORKFLOW THAT CAUSES IT, CORRECTED: app-builder's build.yml - which EVERY app calls - now has a demo job that FAILS when the demo is not the app, so the change that causes the drift is the change that fixes it. RE-SWEPT THE ESTATE with the exact check: 20 demos match their app, 1 had drifted (smartbill), so the class was small but my first sweep had under-counted it.

lessons-smartbill-guards (owner: the pipeline of the total workflow related to forge needs this correction too; smartbill can be improved by adding a person's GSTIN in settings that prints on the bill; from now on write down everything learnt to a repo; also implement in the giant workflow for the forge dashboard and control panel). (1) LEARNINGS.md WRITTEN: LESSONS.md is generated and says 'do not edit by hand', so the hand-written counterpart now exists - eight lessons, each with the evidence that produced it, led by the one that covers most of today: A THING THAT ISN'T WIRED LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE A THING THAT IS. (2) THE FORGE FAMILY CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED: dashboard, control-panel, the hub, Matneo, forge and app-builder have NO source/docs pairs - the demo-drift class CANNOT occur there, so there was nothing to 'fix'. (3) THE GIANT WORKFLOW: the plan now carries four GUARDS as part of the pipeline rather than as habits - the workflow schema, the demo is the app, one licence everywhere, and a spec before a scaffold - each with what it catches and WHY it exists, and the panel shows them. (4) SMARTBILL: the Customer GSTIN already existed, validated and printing on the bill; the gap was retyping it every invoice, so it now has a SAVED-CUSTOMER MASTER - save once, pick from a dropdown, and the name, GSTIN, address and place of supply fill themselves. Matching is by name, so a repeat customer is updated rather than duplicated. The demo was regenerated in the same commit, because the guard added today would rightly have failed the build.

learnings-and-next-app (owner: keep lessons at ONE place, updated with everything found, repeat mistakes / errors / corrections, ADDED WITH COUNT, and solved in the workflow too; then move to the next app). LEARNINGS.md IS NOW THE ONE PLACE: the decision record, distinct from the generated LESSONS.md profile, with each lesson carrying its evidence, an OCCURRENCE COUNT, the guard that closes it and where that guard lives. Four are closed with a named check; the honest state is visible at a glance - THE READ-BACK HAS LIED SIX TIMES with no guard beyond a habit, and 'a thing that isn't wired looks exactly like a thing that is' has happened SEVEN times and is only partially guarded. registry/learnings.json holds the same machine-readably so a count is never retyped by hand. NEXT APP - app-panchang - AND IT FOUND LESSON 1 AGAIN: its spec was marked 'READY - from the idea's own build prompt' and its entire body was the tagline 'daily Indian almanac; enormous, underserved, culturally central.' The APP is far better than that spec (tithi, nakshatra, yoga, karana, vaara, rahu-kaal, sun times, muhurat, with 19 tests verifying Holi 2026-03-03 and Diwali 2026-11-08). An audit of all 154 specs found EIGHT such taglines; all eight now have real specs, and new-app.yml refuses to scaffold a spec under 400 bytes - the guard, so the count stops rising.

mobile-versions-hub (owner: the dashboard still has errors on mobile; improve the control panel; refresh drsamonline.github.io; then back to apps - consolidate in batches, more apps at once if smaller, to improve version and licence). (1) THE DASHBOARD ON MOBILE: the cause was NINE TABLES AND NO OVERFLOW HANDLING - any wide table pushed the WHOLE PAGE sideways, which reads as 'errors' because the layout falls apart rather than because anything throws. Every table is now wrapped in a scroller that scrolls inside itself, and body text wraps anywhere so a long URL cannot widen the page either. (2) THE CONTROL PANEL had the same problem - same hand, same day - and got the same fix. (3) THE HUB: refresh-hub.yml dispatched (my first attempt used the wrong workflow name; the repo has exactly one). (4) THE APPS IN BATCHES: 35 of 36 versioned and changelogged in one pass - 26 had NO VERSION AT ALL, so the licence change had nothing to be released under and was never downloadable. Each now carries a version and a changelog entry naming the licence and the demo rule. HMS returned an HTML error and was retried separately.

panel-css (owner: improve the control panel). THE FINDING WAS NOT WHAT I EXPECTED. I went in to do a responsive pass and found the page had NO CSS FOR ITS LAYOUT CLASSES AT ALL: grid2, ctrls, box, panel, iconbtn, mut and chip are all used in the markup and were defined nowhere. So the panel was rendering as an unstyled column of blocks at EVERY width - not a mobile bug but a missing stylesheet, which is why it looked worst on a phone (where an unstyled column is most obvious) and why a responsive pass alone would have fixed nothing. This is lesson 1 again: the classes EXISTED and did nothing, and 'the class is there' read as 'the class is styled'. ADDED: the real grid2, the Run buttons as a wrapping row, the collapsible boxes with a marker, the finding cards with their ok/bad edge, tables that read narrow, overflow-wrap on the repo names and workflow keys so a long identifier cannot widen the page - and the responsive rules it never had (760px collapses the two columns, 520px tightens the tables). VERIFIED: the classes now have rules and two media queries exist; the visual cannot be checked here, so that is the honest limit.

readback-guard-hms (owner: go - the read-back guard, then HMS). (1) THE READ-BACK LESSON IS CLOSED, and honestly: the count is SIX and it went up TWICE AFTER I wrote the entry, which is why it says six and not four. The guard is now named rather than implied - EVERY WRITE IS VERIFIED AT THE COMMIT SHA, never by re-reading main: list the commits for the path, then read the content at that sha. That is the habit that proved every fix today, including the ones the read-back said had failed. (2) HMS: the cause was found and it was NOT the repo. My commit tried to rewrite CHANGELOG.md, which is 114 KB, and the API answered with an HTML error page twice. Writing the VERSION alone - the part the release actually needs - SUCCEEDED first try, which isolates the cause to the payload size. So the VERSION is in (0.0.2) and the changelog needs a different route: a CI commit, or a new dated file rather than a rewrite of a 114 KB one. That is a real API limit, not a repo fault, and it is worth recording because 'the write failed' looked like a permission problem for two attempts.

hms-proprietary (owner: HMS is proprietary software I am building, so do accordingly). AUDITED THE POSTURE INSTEAD OF ASSUMING THE LICENCE RESTORE WAS ENOUGH, and it was already right: HMS carries its OWN EULA - HHMS, PROPRIETARY SOFTWARE LICENSE AGREEMENT, Version 1.0, effective 12 October 2026, Copyright (c) 2026 Dr. Sohil Momin, Vadodara, all rights reserved - which is NOT PolyForm and was correctly restored when the blanket conversion was reverted. The README says proprietary. There is NO public demo (no docs/play/), so the demo guard does not apply and no preview is published. It uses its own release.yml rather than build-apps.yml, so it is never swept into the open apps' rolling app-latest releases. And registry/licence-policy.json lists it as a deliberate licence, which the licence tool reads BEFORE it touches anything. So the system already treats it as a product - that was not luck, it was the policy written after the blanket conversion mistake. THE ONE GAP: its changelog is 114 KB and rewriting it failed twice, so the 0.0.2 release notes are a dated file of their own, which is the right shape for a product anyway - the changelog keeps its history and each release has its own page.

batch-app-improvements (owner: take MORE apps in one go rather than each app). I STOPPED DOING THEM ONE AT A TIME AND AUDITED ALL 22 APPS FOR THE SAME DEFECTS AT ONCE. That is a better method for its own reason: it shows which defect is COMMON and therefore worth fixing, and which is a one-off not worth a pass. THE AUDIT: 19 of 22 had NO SELF-TEST, 15 no export, 8 a fixed width of 300px+, 3 no viewport, 1 a table with no overflow, 1 an input without a label. So the work is a class, not an app. FIXED IN TWO BATCHES. (1) THE MOBILE CLASS, 6 apps: a viewport where it was missing, fixed widths turned into maximums so they can shrink, and a table wrapper so a wide table scrolls inside itself - the same class that made the dashboard and the control panel look broken on a phone. (2) THE SMOKE TEST, 19 apps: nothing anywhere could tell you whether an app still worked. It is a SMOKE test and called that - did the page come up, are the kits loaded, does storage work - because a feature test needs the feature, and that is not batchable. Open any app with ?test to see it. STILL OPEN: 15 apps have no way to get data OUT (no export), which is the next batch, and it is the one that matters most to a user.

batch-export (owner: continue). THE LAST BIG ABSENCE FROM THE AUDIT: 15 of 22 apps had NO WAY TO GET YOUR DATA OUT. For an offline app that promises the data stays on your device, being unable to leave with it is the sharpest contradiction in the estate - 'your data stays yours' is a claim you cannot act on. FIXED IN ONE PASS: 15 apps (plus the kit demo pages) now have one button and one function that exports the RAW STORE as JSON. IT IS CALLED A BACKUP, NOT A REPORT, because that is what it is - a formatted CSV needs the app's own model, and this is the honest thing that can be identical in every app. Where export-kit is present it uses Export.save; otherwise a plain blob download. It is reachable three ways: the button, ?export in the URL, or window.__exportAll(). THE AUDIT'S CLASSES ARE NOW ALL ADDRESSED: self-test 19 -> 0, export 15 -> 0, mobile widths 8 -> fixed, viewport 3 -> 0. That is what the batch method was for - the same four defects would have taken 45 single-app passes.

coverage-audit (owner: continue). I AUDITED SPECS AGAINST WHAT IS BUILT, AND THE FIRST RUN WAS WRONG - 'BUILT: 2' of 153, which cannot be true. The cause was an ABSENT INPUT: my repo list was a cached file that the recycled sandbox had removed, so the match ran against almost nothing and returned a confident answer. That is lesson 9 exactly - an absence produced a number instead of an error. RE-RAN against the control panel's inventory (69 repos, read from the repo itself) and the real answer is 6 of 153 built from the list: panchang, today-card, canteen-lan, chalk-lan, helioprism, app-encrypted-case-log. THE HONEST FRAMING: the master list is a FORWARD PLAN, and the built estate predates it - bmi, conqueror-os, skin-case-tracker, neon-runner and the rest are apps that were built BEFORE the list existed, so a small overlap is the expected shape, not a failure. What matters is that all 153 now have READY specs, so the auto-build has 147 buildable ideas queued rather than a wall.

deadcode-guard-rejected (owner: the 147 go last, do the remaining first). THE BIGGEST REMAINING ITEM WAS LESSON 1 AT x8 WITH A PARTIAL GUARD, so I built the check for it: a dead-code scan across the estate. IT REPORTED 273 UNREFERENCED FUNCTIONS AND ALMOST ALL WERE WRONG - HMS's buildClinicalBatch is called from another file, frame-kit's `next` is called by the kits' CONSUMERS rather than inside the kit. The scan read one file at a time; these apps are multi-file, so it found the boundary of my method rather than a defect. I DID NOT SHIP IT. A guard that reports 273 false findings is one someone switches off in a week, which is lesson 5 exactly - and I was about to repeat that mistake while writing the lesson about it. LEARNINGS UPDATED: lesson 5 goes to x3 with this as the third occurrence, and lesson 1 records what was tried and rejected and why the honest guard is still the habit plus the tests. The remaining items now: lesson 8 (a fix sharing the bug's blind spot, x2), lesson 9 (absence, x1), the panel's rendering (needs the owner's eyes, not mine), and the specs-vs-implementations quality audit - the coverage audit is done, the 'does each built app do what its spec says' one is not.

batch-import (owner: we were working on enhancements and I wanted them in batches). BACK ON THE ENHANCEMENTS, IN A BATCH. The previous batch gave 15 apps a data export and left an obvious hole: THE FILE IT WRITES COULD NEVER BE READ BACK. A backup you cannot restore is not a backup - it is a souvenir. So 14 apps now have the other half: pick a backup, SEE WHAT IS IN IT BEFORE ANYTHING IS WRITTEN (it lists the keys and the count), confirm, restore, reload. It refuses a file that is not JSON, one with no stored data, and an empty backup, and it asks before replacing what is there now - an import that silently overwrites is worse than no import. Reachable from the button, ?import, or window.__importAll(). THE BATCHES SO FAR: mobile (6 apps), smoke test (19), data export (15), restore (14) - four classes, four passes, instead of fifty single-app visits.

batch-undo (owner: enhancements, in batches). I AUDITED FIRST, AS I SAID I WOULD: 23 of 42 apps looked undo-safe by the test (one write path, a save function). BUT THE TEST WAS A SIGNAL, NOT A PROOF, and a per-app undo needs the app to funnel its writes through one function - where it does not, the undo would QUIETLY DO NOTHING, which is the exact failure this estate keeps producing. SO I CHANGED THE APPROACH RATHER THAN THE APPS: the undo hooks the ONE thing every app shares, localStorage.setItem. It wraps that single function, remembers the previous value of whatever is written, and Ctrl+Z (or the button) restores it and reloads. IT CANNOT SILENTLY DO NOTHING - if the app saves, this sees it. That is lesson 1 applied as a design constraint rather than a warning. Detail worth keeping: Ctrl+Z is ignored while a text field has focus, so the field's own text undo still works. ADDED TO 14 APPS, the ones already carrying the export/import instrumentation. FIVE BATCHES NOW: mobile (6), smoke test (19), export (15), restore (14), undo (14).
machinery check: 39 workflows, 2 scheduled, 15 errors, 0 not firing

batch-keyboard (owner: go). KEYBOARD ACCESS, BATCHED THE SAME WAY: hooked at DOCUMENT, not at each app's internals - the same reasoning as the undo hooking the store. `/` focuses search, `?` shows the shortcuts, Esc leaves a field, and it NEVER STEALS A KEY WHILE A FIELD HAS FOCUS, because a shortcut that eats your typing is a bug wearing a feature's clothes. Also a real :focus-visible ring - most of these apps removed the default outline and never replaced it, so a keyboard user had no idea where they were; a keyboard you cannot see is not access. ADDED TO 14 APPS. THE HONEST GAP THIS EXPOSES: every batch since the export has been gated on the app already carrying the export instrumentation, so the SAME 14 apps now have export, restore, undo AND keyboard - and the other ~28 have none of the four. The batches converged on a subset instead of covering the estate, which is the opposite of what batching was for. NEXT: run all four snippets against the repos that were skipped, which is one pass rather than four.

batch-coverage (owner: go). THE GAP I FLAGGED LAST TIME, CLOSED: every batch since the export had been gated on the app already carrying the export instrumentation, so the SAME 14 apps got export, restore, undo and keyboard while ~28 got nothing. This was the coverage pass - all four in ONE insertion, against the repos that had been skipped: 28 MORE APPS. THE COUNT THAT MATTERS (not what I added, what is THERE): 42 apps have a page, export 40, restore 40, undo 40, keyboard 41. THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE between the batches that looked successful and a batch that actually covered the estate - the first counts additions, the second counts presence. Worth recording as its own lesson: A BATCH THAT REPORTS SUCCESS AGAINST ITS OWN FILTER HAS PROVED NOTHING ABOUT THE ESTATE.

the-five-skipped. THE 100% WAS WRONG AND I HAVE TO SAY SO. The batches and the coverage count both defined 'an app' as a repo with index.html or app.html. runs.note: enumerate-not-define. I STOPPED DEFINING 'AN APP' AND STARTED ENUMERATING THE REPOS. The old filter looked for index.html or app.html; enumerating 69 repos and asking each page WHAT IT IS found 47 apps - and 22 keep their page at src/index.html, frontend/index.html, demo/index.html, chronicles/index.html, sidebar.html or dead-zone/index.html, none of which any batch had ever opened. SO THE '100%' WAS 25 OF 47. Fixed 18 that are genuinely apps; 4 were pages or tools where a 'save my data' button does not belong. LESSON 3 WAS THE PATTERN AND THIS IS THE CORRECTION: a filter is a definition, and a definition written in advance can exclude the thing you care about. runs.note: kit-test-failure (owner: the dashboard has one failed task regarding kit test, what is that). ANSWER: THE FAILURE IS IN DISCOVERY, NOT IN ANY KIT. `All kit tests` has failed on every run since 2026-10-24 because the discover job runs `gh api --paginate --slurp --jq ...`, and gh rejects that pairing outright: 'the `--slurp` option is not supported with `--jq` or `--template`'. The job exits 1, the matrix is never built, and the test job is SKIPPED - so the dashboard reads 'All kit tests - failure' while NOT ONE KIT TEST EVER RAN. THE WORST PART: that workflow's header says 'FIXED (2026-10-24)' with three lines explaining the repair, and it was MY fix that introduced this while fixing a real bug in the same step. A comment claiming FIXED sat above a command that cannot run. FIXED: ask for the names with --paginate --jq (supported together), then build the JSON array with jq; the empty-matrix guard stays so a discovery failure says so instead of looking like a broken kit. Dispatched the workflow to prove it. LESSON 1 GOES TO x9.

specs-vs-implementation (owner: go). THE AUDIT I HAVE BEEN PUTTING OFF, AND IT FOUND THE REAL GAP: for the six apps built from the master list, does the app's own test verify what its spec says DONE MEANS? ONE OF SIX. app-panchang is the good one - its test-node.js names Holi 2026-03-03 and Diwali 2026-11-08 exactly as the spec says. app-encrypted-case-log has a real self-test but not that fact. helioprism tests something else. canteen-lan and chalk-lan have done-means reading 'the self-test in the page passes', which is CIRCULAR - true the moment any test exists. today-card has NO TEST AT ALL. AND THE WORSE FINDING IS IN THE SPECS: a done-means that describes the ACT of testing instead of the FACT being tested cannot fail for the wrong reason, so it certifies nothing. The fix is not more tests - it is a done-means naming an outcome a stranger could check: a date, a count, a value. LESSON 10.

falsifiable-done-means (owner: go). THE FIVE DONE-MEANS ARE REWRITTEN to outcomes a stranger can check: exactly four slots and zero for an empty day; an item reaching a second device on the LAN within five seconds with the internet off; a stroke surviving a reload; exactly three alternatives no two identical; a case absent from the raw store and failing on a wrong passphrase. AND TODAY-CARD TURNED UP SOMETHING BETTER THAN A MISSING TEST: ITS SPEC AND ITS APP WERE DIFFERENT APPS. The spec said weather, the first event, one task, one intention. The app has the date, one intention, one task and a streak. Nothing noticed because nothing had ever compared them - which is what a done-means that cannot fail also hides. The spec now describes the app that exists, and the app has its first real test: the four things by id, today's record agreeing with the fields, and the streak shown equalling the consecutive count computed independently. LESSON 10 TO x2.

four-apps-combined (owner: go in combined batches, finish 4 apps). THE FOUR REMAINING, IN ONE PASS, AND ONLY ONE NEEDED A TEST. app-encrypted-case-log ALREADY VERIFIES ITS SPEC - its runSelfTests check that the passphrase is not in the header, that a DEK is wrapped and that the recovery code is 24 words, which is the done-means. helioprism IS A DIFFERENT APP: its h1 says 'One app. Two kinds of light' with Select files / Start transfer / Save all - a FILE-TRANSFER app, and there is no framing logic in it at all, because the 'Prism' idea-splitter was never built. Its spec now describes what exists. And canteen and chalk have a done-means that NEEDS TWO DEVICES ON A LAN, which no in-page test can prove - so their specs now say so and give the manual check, rather than implying a test that cannot exist. SO THE FOUR WERE: one already correct, one spec describing a different app, two specs whose check needs hardware they cannot reach. LESSON 10 TO x3, with three distinct shapes: circular, never-built, and uncheckable.

queue-spec-audit (owner: go). I AUDITED ALL 154 APP SPECS BY THE THREE SHAPES FOUND TODAY, AND THE ANSWER IS THE QUEUE ITSELF. Only 35 (23%) name an outcome a stranger can check. 41 (27%) are CIRCULAR - 'the self-test in the page passes'. 77 (50%) are TAGLINES with no number and nothing checkable. One has no done-means at all. So 77% of the queue cannot fail for the wrong reason, which means building the 147 as they stand would produce 147 apps that cannot demonstrate they work - the same defect I spent today finding in six apps, waiting in 147 more. THE HONEST CONCLUSION: fixing the done-means is a PREREQUISITE for the queue, not polish after it. The pattern is consistent enough to be mechanical for the taglines - each spec already states its job, so the done-means can be derived from it as an outcome with a number or a named condition - but the circular ones need the app's own domain to say what the test should prove.

done-means-batch (owner: go). I STARTED THE FIX FOR THE 77% AND NEARLY COMMITTED THE BUG AS ITS REMEDY: a programmatic rewrite of the 77 taglines would have produced 'the app does what its job says' - the same circular shape in new words. So 19 were rewritten BY HAND from their own jobs, and only the ones I authored, because I know what they are meant to do: six points on a chart; a contrast ratio to two decimals matching the WCAG formula by hand; one changed word producing ONE highlighted run, not two; ten cron times each at 05:00; FF and 11111111 in the same view; a dose card that REFUSES to compute when the units disagree; an expiry marked Expired before today; a receipt whose amount in words matches the figures; a clash that cannot be saved; a wrong passphrase that fails rather than showing partial data. THE REMAINING 99 NEED THEIR APP'S DOMAIN, and guessing would be worse than leaving them - a fabricated done-means is more dangerous than an honest tagline, because it looks checkable.

kit-tests-two-bugs (owner sent the run URL 40181375393). THAT RUN CONFIRMS THE FAILING TASK IS 'All kit tests', AND THERE WERE TWO BUGS, ONE HIDING THE OTHER. (1) DISCOVERY: gh rejects --slurp with --jq, so the matrix was never built and NO KIT TEST EVER RAN. Fixed earlier today; the dispatched run proves it - discover succeeded and 19 kits actually executed. (2) THE REAL FAILURE THAT WAS HIDDEN: 18 kits passed and ui-kit failed with 'Cannot find module jsdom', because the job runs `node test-node.js` and NEVER RUNS `npm install`. A kit with a dependency could never pass; the other 18 need nothing, which is why it went unseen. Fixed with an install step that warns rather than hard-fails if the install itself breaks. THE DASHBOARD SAID THE SAME THING BOTH TIMES - 'All kit tests - failure' was true for the wrong reason and then for a right one, and the label could not tell you which. LESSON 11: one failure can hide another; a red job is a claim, not a diagnosis.
